stem:
Stimulus: Glucose and galactose are monosaccharides with the same molecular formula, C6H12O6. They differ only in the orientation of the hydroxyl group on carbon 4, which points in opposite directions in the two sugars. A transport protein in the plasma membrane of a bacterium moves galactose into the cell efficiently but moves glucose across the membrane very poorly.

Question: Which statement best explains how this transport protein can distinguish between the two sugars?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Galactose is a disaccharide, so a different kind of transport protein is required than the one that moves glucose.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Galactose contains more carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms than glucose, so the transport protein binds it more strongly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are isomers, and one hydroxyl group's different orientation gives each sugar a different shape, so only galactose fits the binding site.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Galactose carries an extra hydroxyl group that glucose lacks, and the transport protein specifically recognizes that additional group.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Galactose is a monosaccharide, like glucose, not a disaccharide.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The stimulus states that both sugars have the molecular formula C6H12O6, so their atom counts are identical.
rationales.C: Correct. Isomers have the same atoms in different spatial arrangements, so they have different three-dimensional shapes, and a transport protein's binding site can fit one and not the other.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Both sugars have the same number of hydroxyl groups; what differs is the orientation of the one on carbon 4.

stem:
Stimulus: Glucose and mannose are monosaccharides with the same molecular formula, C6H12O6. They differ only in the orientation of the hydroxyl group on carbon 2. A protein on the surface of a bacterium attaches tightly to mannose on the surface of host cells but attaches only weakly to glucose.

Question: Which statement best explains how this protein can distinguish between the two sugars?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are isomers, and one hydroxyl group's different orientation gives each sugar a different shape, so only mannose fits the binding site.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only mannose has a hydroxyl group on carbon 2, and the protein must make direct contact with that specific group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mannose has a different molecular formula than glucose, so its atoms interact differently with the protein's binding site.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glucose is a polysaccharide, so it is too large to fit into the binding site of the protein on the bacterium.

rationales.A: Correct. Isomers have the same atoms in different arrangements, which gives them different three-dimensional shapes and lets a binding site discriminate between them.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Both sugars have a hydroxyl group on carbon 2; the difference is how it is oriented.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The stimulus states that both sugars have the molecular formula C6H12O6, so they contain the same atoms.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Glucose is a monosaccharide, not a polysaccharide.

stem:
Stimulus: A soluble bacterial enzyme normally stays dissolved even at high concentration. A mutant form has a single amino acid substitution in which a surface-exposed threonine (polar, uncharged) is replaced by isoleucine (nonpolar, hydrophobic). At high concentration the mutant enzyme forms insoluble clumps, while the normal enzyme does not. Both forms fold into the same overall three-dimensional shape and are fully active when dissolved.

Question: Which best explains why the mutant enzyme forms clumps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Isoleucine's larger side chain disrupts the enzyme's overall fold, so the mutant partly unfolds and tangles with other enzyme molecules in solution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isoleucine forms ionic bonds between separate enzyme molecules, linking them together in a way that threonine cannot.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The substitution damages the enzyme's catalytic site, and the resulting loss of activity makes the protein precipitate out of solution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The exposed nonpolar isoleucine side chains on different enzyme molecules associate through hydrophobic interactions, away from the surrounding water.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The stimulus states that both forms fold into the same overall shape; the change acts through the surface chemistry, not through unfolding.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Isoleucine's R group is nonpolar, not charged, so it cannot form ionic interactions between enzyme molecules.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The stimulus states that the mutant is fully active when dissolved; clumping is not caused by loss of catalytic function.
rationales.D: Correct. A nonpolar group on the protein's surface tends to avoid water and to associate with nonpolar groups on other molecules, which can build insoluble aggregates without changing each protein's fold.

stem:
Stimulus: A therapeutic protein tends to clump when stored at high concentration. The clumping occurs through contacts between nonpolar leucine side chains that are exposed on the protein's surface. Engineers make a single substitution that replaces one of these surface leucines with glutamate (negatively charged at physiological pH). The modified protein folds into the same shape and stays dissolved at high concentration.

Question: Which best explains why the substitution reduces clumping?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glutamate is also nonpolar, so it strengthens the hydrophobic core and stabilizes the protein against clumping.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glutamate's charged side chain interacts with water and repels neighboring proteins, which removes a nonpolar contact that held molecules together.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glutamate forms covalent peptide bonds with neighboring proteins that lock each protein into a single compact shape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Glutamate makes the protein fold into a smaller shape that buries its other nonpolar groups in the interior.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Glutamate is charged and polar, not nonpolar, and the substituted residue is on the surface, not in the core.
rationales.B: Correct. A charged surface group is favorably hydrated and repels like charges on other molecules, so the hydrophobic contact that drove aggregation is lost.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Peptide bonds link amino acids within a polypeptide chain; a side chain does not form them between separate proteins, and the stimulus says the fold is unchanged.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The stimulus states that the modified protein folds into the same shape as before.

stem:
Stimulus: Two photosynthetic cells are compared under electron microscopy. Cell 1 is approximately 3 μm in diameter and has a single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm and photosynthetic pigments embedded in folded internal membranes. It has no nucleus and no chloroplasts. Cell 2 is approximately 12 μm in diameter and has multiple linear chromosomes inside a double-membrane nucleus and chloroplasts.

Question: Which conclusion about cell classification is most directly supported by the observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both cells are eukaryotic because both are photosynthetic and both contain DNA.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell 1 is eukaryotic because it carries out photosynthesis on internal membranes, which only organelles can provide.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cell 2 is prokaryotic because chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, a process that bacteria also perform.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cell 1 is prokaryotic because it has no nucleus, and Cell 2 is eukaryotic because it has a nucleus and membrane-bound chloroplasts.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes contain DNA, and photosynthesis occurs in both groups, so neither feature classifies a cell.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Some prokaryotes, such as cyanobacteria, photosynthesize on folded internal membranes without having membrane-bound organelles or a nucleus.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Sharing a process does not decide classification; the nucleus, linear chromosomes, 80S ribosomes, and chloroplasts show that Cell 2 is eukaryotic.
rationales.D: Correct. Cell 1 has a circular chromosome in the cytoplasm and no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, which supports prokaryotic classification. Cell 2 has a nucleus, linear chromosomes, and chloroplasts, which support eukaryotic classification.

stem:
Stimulus: A microscopist compares two single-celled organisms. Organism 1 is approximately 1 μm long and has one circular chromosome in a region of cytoplasm with no surrounding membrane, a small circular plasmid, and a peptidoglycan cell wall. Organism 2 is approximately 6 μm in diameter and has linear chromosomes enclosed in a nuclear envelope, mitochondria, and a cell wall made of chitin.

Question: Which conclusion about how these organisms should be classified is most directly supported by the observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Organism 1 is prokaryotic because its DNA lacks a surrounding membrane, and Organism 2 is eukaryotic because it has a nucleus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both organisms are prokaryotic because both are single-celled, and single-celled organisms are always prokaryotes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Organism 2 is prokaryotic because it has a cell wall, just as Organism 1 does, and cell walls are a prokaryotic feature.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Organism 1 is eukaryotic because it has two separate DNA molecules, the main chromosome and a small plasmid, in the same cell.

rationales.A: Correct. A chromosome in an unbounded region of cytoplasm indicates a prokaryote. A nuclear envelope and mitochondria indicate a eukaryote.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Many eukaryotes, such as yeast, are single-celled; cell number does not decide classification.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Cell walls occur in prokaryotes, fungi, and plants, so a wall does not decide classification; the nucleus and mitochondria show that Organism 2 is eukaryotic.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Many prokaryotes carry plasmids; being eukaryotic depends on having a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, not on the number of DNA molecules.

stem:
Stimulus: A student weighs potato cores before and after placing them in solutions for 60 minutes. A core in distilled water gains 9% in mass and becomes stiff. A core in 0.2 M sucrose changes very little in mass. A core in 0.8 M sucrose loses 18% of its mass and becomes limp. The student notes that the core in distilled water stops gaining mass after about 45 minutes and that its cells do not burst.

Question: Which best explains why the core in distilled water stops gaining mass and its cells do not burst?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Water keeps entering until the solute concentration inside the cells equals that of distilled water, and then net movement stops.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The plasma membranes of the potato cells become impermeable to water once the core is stiff, so osmosis stops.

choices.label: C
choices.text: As water enters, the cell wall resists expansion and turgor pressure rises until it opposes further net water entry.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Potato cells have the same solute concentration as distilled water, so they neither gain nor lose water.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The cell contents never become as dilute as pure water. Net movement stops when rising turgor pressure counteracts the osmotic gradient.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The membranes remain permeable to water. Net water movement stops because turgor pressure balances the osmotic gradient, not because the membrane blocks water.
rationales.C: Correct. Distilled water is hypotonic to the cells, so water enters by osmosis. The wall resists expansion, and the resulting turgor pressure balances the tendency of water to enter, so net movement stops before the membrane ruptures.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The core in distilled water gained 9% in mass, so water entered; distilled water is hypotonic to the cells. The solution that changed the mass very little (0.2 M sucrose) is the one closest to isotonic.

stem:
Stimulus: A student mounts onion epidermal tissue in distilled water and views it under a microscope. The cells are firm, and the plasma membrane presses against the cell wall. The student replaces the water with a 1 M salt solution. Within minutes the cells shrink, and in the corners of each cell the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall, leaving gaps. The plasma membrane remains intact.

Question: Which best explains why the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall in the salt solution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cell wall contracts when it contacts the salt solution and pulls itself away from the plasma membrane.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Water leaves the cells by osmosis toward the more concentrated solution, so the cell contents shrink while the rigid wall keeps its shape.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salt enters the cells and dissolves the cell wall, which releases the plasma membrane from its surface.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Active transport pumps water out of the cells against its concentration gradient, which shrinks the cell contents.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The wall is rigid and does not contract; it is the cell contents inside the wall that decrease in volume.
rationales.B: Correct. Water moves out of the cells toward the more concentrated solution, so the volume of the cell contents decreases. The rigid cell wall does not shrink with them, which leaves a gap.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Salt does not dissolve the cellulose cell wall, and the wall is still present in the observation; it is the cell contents that shrink.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Water crosses membranes passively by osmosis, down its concentration gradient; cells do not actively pump water.

stem:
Stimulus: Developing red blood cells take in iron by endocytosis. Iron-bound transferrin, a protein in the blood, binds to transferrin receptors, which are proteins in the plasma membrane. The membrane then folds inward and engulfs the bound transferrin in a vesicle that carries the iron into the cell. A rare inherited mutation prevents transferrin receptors from reaching the plasma membrane of developing red blood cells.

Question: Which prediction about individuals with this mutation is best supported by the described process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron-bound transferrin will stay in the blood at high levels, because the cells have no receptors to bind it and take it in.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cells will have more iron available inside, because the iron stays outside the cells, where it can diffuse freely into the cytoplasm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron-bound transferrin will cross the phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion instead, because the receptors are not needed for uptake.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The plasma membrane will stop folding inward in these cells, so no other substance can be taken in by endocytosis.

rationales.A: Correct. In the process described, uptake starts when transferrin binds a receptor in the plasma membrane. Without receptors at the surface, the cells cannot take in the transferrin, so it stays in the blood.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Iron bound to transferrin does not diffuse freely across the hydrophobic interior of the membrane. Without the receptor, the iron is not taken into the cells.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Transferrin is a large protein, and the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer blocks large and polar substances. In the process described, uptake depends on the receptor and endocytosis.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The mutation removes only the transferrin receptor from the surface. The cells can still carry out endocytosis for substances whose receptors are present.

stem:
Stimulus: Liver cells remove LDL particles, which carry cholesterol, from the blood by endocytosis. LDL binds to receptor proteins in the plasma membrane, and the binding makes the membrane fold inward and engulf the LDL in a vesicle. A mutant form of the receptor reaches the plasma membrane and binds LDL as well as the normal receptor does, but it cannot make the membrane fold inward.

Question: Which prediction about liver cells that have only the mutant receptor is best supported by the described process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cells will take in LDL normally, because binding to the receptor is the only step in uptake that needs a receptor protein.

choices.label: B
choices.text: LDL will bind to the surface of the cells but will not be taken in, so the level of LDL in the blood will stay high.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fewer receptors will reach the plasma membrane, so the cells will bind less LDL than normal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: LDL will cross the phospholipid bilayer directly once it is bound to the receptor, so the level of LDL in the blood will fall.

rationales.A: Incorrect. In the process described, binding makes the membrane fold inward and engulf the LDL. The mutant receptor cannot do this, so uptake does not occur normally.
rationales.B: Correct. The mutant receptor binds LDL, but uptake needs the membrane to fold inward around it. Without that step, the LDL is not engulfed and is not removed from the blood.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The stimulus states that the mutant receptor reaches the plasma membrane and binds LDL as well as the normal receptor does.
rationales.D: Incorrect. LDL particles are too large to cross the hydrophobic interior of the bilayer. Without endocytosis, bound LDL is not carried into the cell.

stem:
Stimulus: Pancreatic cells secrete the digestive enzyme amylase. Normally, amylase is made by ribosomes attached to the rough ER, and it then passes through the Golgi complex and transport vesicles before it is secreted from the cell. A researcher treats the cells with a drug that stops ribosomes from attaching to the rough ER. The ribosomes remain in the cytoplasm.

Question: Which outcome for amylase in the treated cells is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amylase moves directly from the cytoplasm into the Golgi complex, where it is modified and then secreted as usual.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amylase is no longer made at all, because only ribosomes attached to the rough ER can carry out protein synthesis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Amylase is still made, but in the cytoplasm rather than at the rough ER, so it does not enter the endomembrane system and little is secreted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Amylase is made on the smooth ER instead and is secreted normally, because the smooth ER also takes part in making proteins.

rationales.A: Incorrect. In the route described, the protein reaches the Golgi complex after it is made at the rough ER. A protein made in the cytoplasm does not skip that step.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Ribosomes in the cytoplasm also synthesize proteins from mRNA, so the enzyme can still be made. It just is not made at the rough ER.
rationales.C: Correct. Ribosomes in the cytoplasm can still make a protein from mRNA, but the protein is not made at the rough ER, so it does not pass through the Golgi complex and vesicles to be secreted.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The smooth ER is involved in detoxification and lipid synthesis. Ribosomes, not the smooth ER, make proteins.

stem:
Stimulus: A pancreatic cell secretes a digestive enzyme. Researchers expose the cells briefly to radioactive amino acids and then follow the radioactive enzyme over time. At first, most of the radioactivity is found in the rough ER. Later it is found in the Golgi complex, then in transport vesicles near the plasma membrane, and finally outside the cell.

Question: Which interpretation of these results is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The smooth ER makes the enzyme, because the rough ER only provides support for the cell and does not take part in making proteins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ribosomes on the rough ER make the enzyme, and it then moves through the Golgi complex and vesicles, where it is modified and packaged for secretion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Golgi complex makes the enzyme from mRNA, and the rough ER later folds it before the enzyme is moved to the plasma membrane.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysosomes receive the enzyme from the rough ER and release it from the cell, because lysosomes are the organelles that secrete enzymes.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Rough ER is the part with membrane-bound ribosomes that helps carry out protein synthesis; smooth ER is involved in detoxification and lipid synthesis.
rationales.B: Correct. Ribosomes synthesize proteins from mRNA, and rough ER has membrane-bound ribosomes. The Golgi complex then folds, modifies, and packages the protein, and vesicles carry it out of the cell.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Ribosomes, not the Golgi complex, synthesize proteins from mRNA, and the radioactivity reached the Golgi complex after the rough ER, not before it.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that digest material; they are not the route for secretion. The radioactivity moved through the Golgi complex and transport vesicles to the outside.

stem:
Stimulus: Evidence supporting the endosymbiotic origin of chloroplasts includes: (1) chloroplasts have a double membrane, with an inner membrane like the plasma membrane of a cyanobacterium and an outer membrane like the host cell's endomembrane; (2) chloroplasts contain their own circular DNA; (3) chloroplasts contain ribosomes made of rRNA and protein, like those of prokaryotes; (4) chloroplasts reproduce independently of the cell cycle of the host.

Question: Which single piece of evidence most specifically supports the claim that a host cell engulfed a cyanobacterium, rather than only showing that chloroplasts have a prokaryote-like ancestry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reproducing independently of the host's cell cycle shows that the chloroplast was surrounded by a host membrane during engulfment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The double membrane, with an inner layer like a cyanobacterial membrane and an outer layer like host endomembrane, matches engulfment by a host vesicle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Having its own circular DNA shows that chloroplasts are still able to survive on their own outside the plant cell.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Having ribosomes made of rRNA and protein shows that each chloroplast is still a free-living cyanobacterium inside the cell.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Independent reproduction shows a similarity to prokaryotes, but it says nothing about a host membrane surrounding the cell. The double membrane is the evidence that does.
rationales.B: Correct. Evidence (1) describes the physical result of engulfment: the inner membrane belongs to the engulfed cell and the outer membrane comes from the host vesicle. The other pieces show prokaryote-like ancestry but not how the cell came to be inside the host.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Circular DNA shows a link to prokaryotes, but it does not show that chloroplasts can survive on their own, and it does not show how they came to be inside the host.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Ribosomes are found in all forms of life and reflect common ancestry. They do not show how the organelle came to be inside the cell or that it is still free-living.

stem:
Stimulus: Two hypotheses explain the origin of chloroplasts. In the endosymbiosis hypothesis, a host cell engulfed a cyanobacterium. In the infolding hypothesis, part of the host's own plasma membrane folded inward and enclosed some of the host's cytoplasm, which later specialized for photosynthesis. Researchers sequence the chloroplast genome and compare it with other genomes. They find that chloroplast genes are circular, lack histones, and are more similar in sequence to genes of modern cyanobacteria than to genes in the plant's own nucleus.

Question: Which conclusion is best supported by the sequence comparison?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because chloroplasts have a double membrane, the sequence data show that they formed by infolding of the host's plasma membrane.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because chloroplasts carry their own DNA, the sequence data show that the host nucleus contributes no genes to chloroplast function.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chloroplast genes are more closely related to cyanobacterial genes than to the host's nuclear genes, which supports endosymbiosis over infolding of the host's membrane.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because chloroplast DNA lacks histones, the sequence data show that chloroplasts are not part of the plant cell.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The sequence comparison says nothing about membrane layers, and a double membrane could be produced by either hypothesis.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Many chloroplast proteins are encoded in the nuclear genome and imported, so the nucleus does contribute to chloroplast function.
rationales.C: Correct. If chloroplasts arose from the host's own membrane and cytoplasm, their genes would resemble the host's. Greater similarity to cyanobacterial genes points to a cyanobacterial origin.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Histone-free DNA is a bacterial feature, but chloroplasts are part of the plant cell and depend on proteins encoded by nuclear genes.
